practice.stem: Hypertrophy is an increase in:
practice.rationale: Hypertrophy = bigger cells, not more cells — "remember, not number, size." More cells is hyperplasia; a change of type is metaplasia; disordered growth is dysplasia.

practice.stem: Hyperplasia is best defined as:
options: Replacement of one mature cell type with another
practice.rationale: Hyperplasia is proliferation — more cells. It can occur together with hypertrophy, which is why the two get confused; atrophy is shrinkage and metaplasia is a type swap.

practice.stem: Which cells cannot undergo hyperplasia?
practice.rationale: Cells that don't divide — cardiac muscle and neurons — can't add cell number, so they only hypertrophy or atrophy. Liver, endometrium and skin all proliferate (liver regrows, warts are skin hyperplasia).

practice.stem: What is the most common cause of cell injury?
practice.rationale: Hypoxia — lack of sufficient oxygen — is the most common cause of cell injury, and ischemia is the most common cause of hypoxia. Free radicals, chemicals and infection are other listed causes.

practice.stem: What is the most common cause of hypoxia?
options: High altitude (low O2 in the air)
practice.rationale: Ischemia is listed as the most common cause of hypoxia. Loss of hemoglobin, low-oxygen air and poisoning are real causes, but less common.

practice.stem: According to the lecture, a normal WBC count is:
practice.rationale: Slide 30 gives 5,000–9,000/mm³. Leukocytosis in acute inflammation is > 10,000; 150,000–400,000 is a platelet range.

practice.stem: Which form of cell death is frequently accompanied by inflammation in adjacent tissue?
practice.rationale: Necrosis spills cell contents and inflames neighbors; apoptosis packages contents into apoptotic bodies with no inflammation. Senescence and atrophy aren't forms of cell death.

practice.stem: Which type of necrosis is classically caused by tuberculosis?
practice.rationale: Caseous necrosis — cheese-like clumps walled off by a granuloma — is usually from TB. Coagulative follows ischemia in organs like the heart; liquefactive is typical of brain and bacterial infection; fat necrosis is breast/pancreas.

practice.stem: Which cell is the most important cellular activator of the inflammatory response?
practice.rationale: The mast cell — a sentinel sitting near vessels — degranulates histamine within seconds. Neutrophils are the first phagocytes to arrive, platelets drive clotting, and B cells are adaptive.

practice.stem: Which phagocytes are the first responders at a site of inflammation?
practice.rationale: Neutrophils arrive first, are short-lived and become pus. Macrophages arrive ~24 h later and replace them; eosinophils are mildly phagocytic; dendritic cells link innate and adaptive immunity.

practice.stem: Which two complement proteins did he call "the big boys"?
practice.rationale: "What I want you guys to know is that C3 and C5 are the big boys of the complement system." CRP and fibrinogen are acute-phase proteins, not complement.

practice.stem: In the clotting system, fibrinogen is converted into:
practice.rationale: He asked you to know fibrinogen → fibrin: fibrinogen circulates inactive and becomes fibrin when bleeding activates the cascade. Bradykinin belongs to the kinin system.

practice.stem: Which cytokines are anti-inflammatory?
practice.rationale: IL-10 and TGF-β suppress lymphocytes and lower pro-inflammatory cytokines, so inflammation shuts off after a few days. IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α are the pro-inflammatory trio.

practice.stem: Acute inflammation is generally defined as lasting:
practice.rationale: Acute is less than 2 weeks; more than 2 weeks is chronic. He noted "some debate whether 2–6 weeks is still acute."

practice.stem: A patient's forearm muscles look visibly smaller after 6 weeks in a cast. This is:
practice.rationale: Not using a muscle shrinks its cells — disuse atrophy (the Kahoot's leg-out-of-a-cast). Denervation needs nerve loss; hypertrophy would be growth; dysplasia is disordered growth.

practice.stem: Which change is pathologic hypertrophy?
options: A thickened left ventricle from long-standing hypertension
A uterus enlarging from hormonal stimulation during pregnancy
A runner's slightly larger heart after years of endurance training
A weight lifter's enlarged biceps after months of training
practice.rationale: The HTN heart is maladaptive — the wall thickens against high pressure until the ventricle can't fill. Exercise-related enlargement is physiologic; pregnancy is hormonal (physiologic) growth.

practice.stem: After a nephrectomy, the remaining kidney enlarges. The best description is:
practice.rationale: Compensatory = a pathologic event (kidney removed) followed by a physiologic response (the other kidney grows cell size to cover the loss).

practice.stem: A long-term smoker's airway loses its ciliated cells, replaced by squamous cells. Which statement is true?
options: It is irreversible necrosis caused by the toxins in cigarette smoke
It is a harmless physiologic adaptation that strengthens and protects the airway lining
It is a maladaptation that removes a protective function and raises cancer risk
It is caused by denervation of the airway after years of smoking
practice.rationale: Metaplasia protects the cells from the irritants they were catching, but now nothing is caught — maladaptation. Switching cell type means genes are up/down-regulated, which can progress to cancer.

practice.stem: Common warts are an example of:
practice.rationale: "Warts is the classic example" of viral, pathologic hyperplasia of skin cells. Physiologic hyperplasia is hormonal (breast, uterus).

practice.stem: Blood flow is restored to an ischemic area of heart muscle, yet more cells die afterward. What explains this?
options: Ischemia-reperfusion injury from oxidative stress, calcium overload, inflammation and complement
Metastatic calcification as calcium salts deposit in the reperfused heart muscle and kill cells
Compensatory hyperplasia as surviving cells divide to replace the dead ones
Apoptosis caused by estrogen loss, the same process that shrinks tissue after menopause
practice.rationale: Reperfusion adds injury when O₂ returns — free radicals, intracellular Ca²⁺, inflammation and complement. His point: a large share of cells die after flow is restored.

practice.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has repeated infections. Which explanation fits the lecture?
options: Mast cells release less histamine, so fewer leukocytes are called in
Too many plasma-derived mediators keep the patient in constant inflammation
IL-10 production is increased, turning the inflammatory response off
The liver makes fewer complement, clotting and kinin proteins
practice.rationale: The plasma-derived systems are made by the liver. A cirrhotic liver makes less complement (less opsonization and lysis), so infection rates rise.

practice.stem: A patient takes aspirin for a headache. How does this reduce inflammation?
options: It increases IL-6, which turns inflammation back off
It activates complement to clear the injured cells
It blocks histamine receptors on the blood vessels
practice.rationale: Aspirin and NSAIDs block the COX pathway from arachidonic acid, lowering prostaglandins (pain, permeability). Corticosteroids act earlier, at membrane phospholipids; antihistamines block histamine.

practice.stem: A patient in septic shock is severely hypotensive. Which mediator is mainly responsible?
practice.rationale: Large amounts of TNF-α cause widespread vasodilation — "that's why we call it septic shock." IL-10 and TGF-β are anti-inflammatory; interferons are antiviral.

practice.stem: A patient with the flu is lethargic, sleepy and has no appetite. These symptoms are driven mainly by:
options: Complement C3 and C5 (opsonization and lysis)
practice.rationale: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α act on the brain to cause sickness behavior. NSAIDs or Tylenol make you "perk up" — the infection isn't gone.

practice.stem: Why did he describe inflammation as nonspecific?
options: It produces the same response no matter what caused the injury
It occurs only in avascular tissue, away from the bloodstream
It targets one specific antigen at a time, like adaptive immunity
It only responds to bacteria, not to physical or chemical injury
practice.rationale: "No matter the injury, it's the same response." Cells don't know the cause, so they go all out — lifesaving for a snake bite, overkill for a sprained ankle.

practice.stem: A patient's tuberculosis infection has persisted for months, with granulomas on imaging. This represents:
practice.rationale: Longer than 2 weeks, the acute response failed, dense lymphocytes and macrophages, granuloma walling it off — TB is the classic chronic example.

practice.stem: An obese patient's abdominal incision separates on post-op day 7. This is:
practice.rationale: Dehiscence is wound separation, highest risk days 5–12, more likely with obesity and abdominal wounds. Contracture is excessive contraction; a keloid is excess scar.

practice.stem: Why does diabetes delay wound healing?
options: It speeds collagen remodeling, so the scar forms before the wound has closed
It increases platelet count, so excess clotting blocks blood flow to the wound
It causes metastatic calcification of the wound bed, which blocks new tissue growth
Small-vessel disease impairs microcirculation and hyperglycemia impairs macrophages
practice.rationale: Diabetes acts like ischemia — capillaries don't work right, and inflammation needs blood flow — and high glucose impairs macrophages and feeds bacteria.

practice.stem: Bronchial biopsy: ciliated columnar epithelium replaced by squamous epithelium. Identify the process.
practice.rationale: One mature cell type swapped for another = metaplasia (the textbook trachea example). Dysplasia would show cells varying in size, shape and organization.

practice.stem: Cervical biopsy: cells vary in size and shape and have lost normal organization. Identify the process.
practice.rationale: Deranged growth with variable size, shape and organization = dysplasia ("atypical hyperplasia"), common in the cervix and respiratory tract.

practice.stem: Microscopy: swollen cells, disrupted membranes, contents leaking, inflammation in surrounding tissue.
practice.rationale: Swelling, disrupted membrane, leaking contents and adjacent inflammation are necrosis. Apoptosis shrinks the cell, keeps the membrane intact, and causes no inflammation.

practice.stem: Microscopy: a shrunken cell, fragmented nucleus, intact membrane, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation.
practice.rationale: Reduced size, nuclear fragmentation, intact membrane and apoptotic bodies without inflammation = apoptosis, programmed cell death.

practice.stem: After a stroke, the infarcted brain tissue softens into a liquid, pus-like mass. Identify the necrosis.
practice.rationale: Ischemic injury to neurons/glia and bacterial infections produce liquefactive necrosis — hydrolytic enzymes digest the tissue. Ischemia in heart or kidney is coagulative instead.

practice.stem: Pancreatitis: chalky white deposits where lipases broke down triglycerides into soaps. Identify the necrosis.
practice.rationale: Lipases split triglycerides; free fatty acids combine with ions to form soap (saponification) — fat necrosis of pancreas or breast.

practice.stem: A toe is black, dry and shrunken after arterial occlusion; no infection is present.
practice.rationale: Ischemia leading to coagulative necrosis gives dry gangrene — dry, shrunken, black/brown. Wet adds infection (cold, wet, pulseless); gas gangrene has crepitus.

practice.stem: An infected leg wound shows crepitus on palpation after a clostridial infection.
practice.rationale: Clostridium toxins make gas bubbles in infected muscle — gas gangrene (myonecrosis), felt as crepitus.

practice.stem: A fresh scrape oozes a thin, clear, watery fluid.
practice.rationale: Early or mild inflammation with few proteins or WBCs gives a watery, serous exudate — his scrape example.

practice.stem: A wound drains thick, opaque fluid full of neutrophils and cellular debris.
practice.rationale: Pus — large numbers of leukocytes (especially neutrophils) and debris — is a purulent exudate.

practice.stem: On day 6, a healing wound bed is beefy red and full of new capillaries, and fibroblasts are laying down collagen.
practice.rationale: Granulation tissue, angiogenesis and fibroblast collagen synthesis define the proliferative phase (days 3–14) — the Kahoot's answer for fibroblasts.

practice.stem: Months after an ear piercing, a firm, raised overgrowth of scar tissue extends beyond the wound.
practice.rationale: Remodeling gone awry, laying down too much scar = keloid. His example: an ear piercing that "kept on healing."

practice.stem: Calcium deposits form in a damaged heart valve; the patient's serum calcium is normal.
practice.rationale: Calcium in injured tissue with normal serum calcium = dystrophic. Metastatic calcification deposits in normal tissue because of hypercalcemia.

practice.stem: Temp 101.8°F, WBC 13,500/mm³, CRP and ESR elevated, 3 days after a large injury.
options: Chronic inflammation walled off by a granuloma
practice.rationale: Fever, leukocytosis > 10,000 and acute-phase reactants (CRP, raised ESR) within days of a big injury are systemic signs of acute inflammation.

clinical.title: Scenario 1 — Pulmonary clinic
clinical.setting: Outpatient visit, follow-up of an abnormal bronchoscopy
clinical.text: A 58-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history has a chronic morning cough. Bronchial biopsy report: ciliated columnar epithelium replaced by stratified squamous epithelium in several areas. He asks the nurse whether this means he has cancer.

questions.stem: Which cellular adaptation does the biopsy describe?
questions.rationale: One mature cell type replaced by another — ciliated columnar to squamous — is metaplasia, driven by chronic irritation. It's a type change, not a change in size or number.

questions.stem: Why did these airway cells lose their cilia?
options: Nicotine directly dissolves the cilia, leaving the cells bare and unable to clear mucus
The cilia trapped the inhaled irritants that injured the cells, so the cells changed to stop catching them
The ciliated cells were dying by apoptosis and were being replaced by scar tissue along the airway lining
Cilia are lost normally with age, and smoking only speeds up this expected change
questions.rationale: His explanation: cilia catch everything inhaled; for a smoker that's toxic, so the cells "get rid of our cilia" to stop grabbing it. It's an adaptation, not cell death or normal aging.

questions.stem: How should the nurse describe this change to the patient?
options: It is a maladaptation that can reverse if he stops smoking, but it can progress toward dysplasia and cancer
It is a healthy adaptation that protects his lungs, so there's no need to change his smoking
It is irreversible cell death, so the damaged airway lining will never recover even if he quits smoking
It is cancer that has already formed in the airway and will spread unless it is removed
questions.rationale: Metaplasia is reversible but maladaptive — nothing gets caught anymore — and switching cell type involves gene up/down-regulation that can progress to dysplasia and neoplasm. Quitting lets cells recover.

questions.stem: A repeat biopsy a year later is being compared. Which findings would indicate progression to dysplasia? Select all that apply.
options: Uniform squamous cells in orderly layers
questions.rationale: Dysplasia = deranged growth — cells varying in size, shape and organization. Uniform orderly squamous cells are still metaplasia; returning cilia means recovery.

clinical.title: Scenario 2 — Cardiology clinic
clinical.text: A 64-year-old woman with uncontrolled hypertension for 15 years reports fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. Echo: markedly thickened left ventricular wall with a small chamber. Her daughter, a marathon runner, was told she also has "a big heart."

questions.stem: Which adaptation is present in the mother's heart?
questions.rationale: Heart cells grow in size working against high blood pressure — pathologic, maladaptive hypertrophy. Cardiac muscle can't divide, so hyperplasia isn't possible.

questions.stem: Why does this adaptation cause her symptoms?
options: The heart cells are dying by apoptosis, so too few muscle cells are left to pump the blood
The ventricle has too many new cells, so it beats too fast to fill
The thick wall leaves too little chamber space for blood to fill the ventricle
The heart has become metaplastic, replacing muscle with weaker cells
questions.rationale: His answer to "why is this a bad thing?": so much hypertrophy that blood can't fill the ventricle — the cells adapt to the pressure but make function worse.

questions.stem: How does the daughter's heart differ?
options: It is cardiac hyperplasia, with more muscle cells added from exercise
It is the same pathologic process, just at an earlier and milder stage
It is compensatory atrophy after her heart adapted to training
It is physiologic hypertrophy from exercise and still fills normally
questions.rationale: Exercise enlarges the heart a little — "not a big deal, it still fills with blood" — physiologic hypertrophy. The pathology comes from working against constant high pressure.

questions.stem: Which statement about cardiac muscle cells is correct?
options: They respond to stress mainly by hyperplasia, adding new cells
They cannot undergo hyperplasia because they don't divide
questions.rationale: Non-dividing cells like cardiac muscle and neurons can't increase in number — they adapt by size (hypertrophy or atrophy).

clinical.title: Scenario 3 — Outpatient rehabilitation
clinical.setting: Two patients on the same afternoon
clinical.text: Patient A, 34, just had a long leg cast removed after 8 weeks; the casted thigh is visibly thinner. Patient B, 41, donated a kidney 6 months ago; imaging shows her remaining kidney is larger than before.

questions.stem: What best explains Patient A's thinner thigh?
questions.rationale: Muscle that isn't used shrinks its cells — disuse atrophy, the Kahoot's leg-after-a-cast. Denervation requires nerve loss.

questions.stem: What best explains the change in Patient B's remaining kidney?
questions.rationale: Removing a kidney is the pathologic event; the remaining kidney enlarging to cover the loss is the physiologic response — together, compensatory.

questions.stem: Which are causes of atrophy listed in the lecture? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Atrophy causes: disuse, denervation, loss of endocrine stimulation, inadequate nutrition, ischemia, aging. Weight-lifting causes hypertrophy; viral infection (warts) causes hyperplasia.

questions.stem: A patient's liver regrows after 70% was removed. How does this compare with Patient B?
options: It is dysplasia — the regrown liver cells vary in size, shape and organization
It is compensatory hyperplasia — cell number increases, rather than cell size
It is metaplasia — one liver cell type is replaced by another
It is the same as Patient B — hypertrophy, with cell size increasing
questions.rationale: Liver regenerates by increasing cell number (compensatory hyperplasia, ~2 weeks after removal of 70%); the kidney example is cell size (hypertrophy).

clinical.title: Scenario 4 — Cardiac care unit
clinical.text: A 61-year-old man had chest pain for 3 hours before an occluded coronary artery was opened. Shortly after blood flow was restored, his cardiac markers rose further. Labs: CK and AST elevated, WBC 11,800/mm³, temp 100.6°F.

questions.stem: Before the artery was opened, what was the main mechanism of injury to his heart cells?
questions.rationale: Ischemia is the most common cause of hypoxia, and hypoxia is the most common cause of cell injury: ATP falls, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump fails, cells swell.

questions.stem: Restoring blood flow can add injury. Which mechanisms of ischemia-reperfusion injury does the lecture list? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Slide 26 lists oxidative stress, increased intracellular Ca²⁺, inflammation and complement activation. Metaplasia is an adaptation; more antioxidants would protect.

questions.stem: Why are CK and AST elevated?
options: The liver is producing them as acute-phase proteins
Injured heart muscle cells release these enzymes
questions.rationale: Injured cells leak enzymes: CK (skeletal muscle, brain, heart) and AST (heart, liver, muscle, kidney, pancreas) are listed systemic signs of cell injury.

questions.stem: Irreversibly injured heart cells here will most likely undergo which type of necrosis?
questions.rationale: Coagulative necrosis occurs in kidneys, heart and adrenals from hypoxia/ischemia — proteins denature into a firm, opaque state. Liquefactive is typical of brain.

questions.stem: His WBC count of 11,800/mm³ and low-grade fever are best explained by:
options: Chronic inflammation from a granuloma walling off injury
Normal values within the expected range
Systemic response to cell injury and inflammation
questions.rationale: Normal WBC is 5,000–9,000; injury causes leukocytosis and fever from endogenous pyrogens. It's hours old, so it isn't chronic.

clinical.title: Scenario 5 — Medical-surgical unit
clinical.text: A 72-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes and peripheral vascular disease has a foot ulcer that hasn't healed in 2 months. The second toe is now cold, swollen, wet-appearing and pulseless, with foul drainage. Blood glucose 312 mg/dL.

questions.stem: Which condition does the toe's appearance suggest?
questions.rationale: Ischemia with superimposed bacterial infection → liquefactive necrosis: cold, wet, pulseless — wet gangrene. Dry gangrene is dry and shrunken; gas gangrene has crepitus.

questions.stem: Which factors in this patient impair wound healing? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Diabetes (microcirculation, hyperglycemia impairs macrophages and feeds bacteria), ischemia and infection are listed dysfunctions; "inflammation needs blood flow." Adequate nutrition helps healing.

questions.stem: The ulcer has persisted for 2 months with ongoing inflammation. This is best classified as:
questions.rationale: More than 2 weeks, with an acute response that failed to resolve the cause and incomplete healing, is chronic inflammation.

questions.stem: If the wound eventually heals as an open wound filling from the base, it heals by:
options: Primary intention — faster, with minimal scarring and infection risk
Hemostasis alone — a fibrin clot seals the wound bed
Metaplasia — new cell types replace the lost tissue
Secondary intention — slower, more scarring, higher infection risk
questions.rationale: Open wounds with tissue loss (like pressure ulcers) heal by secondary intention: slower, more scar, far greater infection risk.

clinical.title: Scenario 6 — Emergency department
clinical.text: Patient A, 25, sprained his ankle playing basketball: swollen, warm, red, painful, and he can't bear weight. Patient B, 30, was bitten by a rattlesnake on the hand an hour ago; the hand and forearm are rapidly swelling.

questions.stem: Which of Patient A's findings are cardinal signs of inflammation? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function are the classic signs. Cyanosis signals hypoxemia, not inflammation.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, for which patient is the full inflammatory response most important?
questions.rationale: His scenario: without inflammation the snake-bite victim might die; the sprained ankle won't die, inflammation just makes the next weeks worse.

questions.stem: Why does the body mount the same intense response to a sprained ankle?
options: Inflammation is nonspecific — cells don't know the cause, so they go all out
The ankle injury releases toxins as dangerous as venom
Sprains always become infected, so a full response is needed
Adaptive immunity directs it, copying the response it learned from earlier injuries
questions.rationale: "No matter the injury, it's always going to be the same response." Cells can't tell a sprain from a bite, so the response is all or nothing.

questions.stem: Put the steps of Patient A's inflammatory response in order.
options: Leukocytes adhere to vessel walls and migrate into the tissue
Vasodilation increases blood flow to the ankle
Leukocytes are activated and phagocytize debris
Vascular permeability increases and fluid leaks out (edema)
questions.rationale: Timeline (the Kahoot): vascular response first — vasodilation, then permeability and exudate — then leukocyte adhesion and migration (chemotaxis), then activation and phagocytosis.

questions.stem: Which phagocytes arrive first at Patient A's injury?
questions.rationale: Neutrophils are the first responders; monocytes/macrophages arrive about 24 h later and take over. B cells and plasma cells are adaptive.

clinical.title: Scenario 7 — Medical unit
clinical.text: A 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis is admitted with his third skin infection this year. Labs: low albumin, prolonged clotting times, WBC 12,900/mm³. He asks why he "keeps catching everything."

questions.stem: Which explanation is best supported by the lecture?
options: His liver makes too much complement, which attacks his own healthy cells and weakens his defenses
His liver makes fewer plasma-derived proteins such as complement, so his defenses are weaker
Cirrhosis increases IL-10, which turns off his inflammatory response to infection
His mast cells can't release histamine, so leukocytes are never called in
questions.rationale: The complement, clotting and kinin systems are made by the liver. His answer: a cirrhotic liver means decreased complement → less opsonization and lysis → more infections.

questions.stem: Complement normally helps phagocytes by:
options: Opsonization — marking bacteria so phagocytes can recognize and eat them
Producing antibodies that bind bacteria so phagocytes can find them
Dissolving fibrin clots so phagocytes can travel into the infected tissue
Lowering body temperature so phagocytes work more efficiently
questions.rationale: "Placing a marker on the bacteria" — opsonization. Without it, bacteria are harder for phagocytes to find. Antibodies come from B/plasma cells.

questions.stem: Which are actions of activated complement (C3 and C5)? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Slide 60: opsonization, anaphylatoxic activity, leukocyte chemotaxis, cell lysis. Complement amplifies inflammation; it isn't anti-inflammatory.

questions.stem: His prolonged clotting times fit which fact about the clotting system?
options: Clotting proteins like fibrinogen are plasma-derived and made by the liver
Fibrin is made by neutrophils, which a cirrhotic patient has too few of
Clotting factors come from mast cells, which degranulate less in cirrhosis
Platelets make fibrinogen, and cirrhosis lowers the platelet count
questions.rationale: Fibrinogen and the other clotting proteins circulate from the liver and are activated at injury; less liver function means less of them.

clinical.title: Scenario 8 — Intensive care unit
clinical.text: A 67-year-old woman with a urinary tract infection becomes confused, febrile (103.1°F) and hypotensive (78/40) with warm, flushed skin. Blood cultures are drawn; the team suspects septic shock. Her daughter says she's been "lethargic and not eating for two days."

questions.stem: Which cytokine is the main problem in septic shock?
questions.rationale: TNF-α is highly inflammatory; large amounts in bacteremia cause widespread vasodilation → shock. IL-10 and TGF-β are anti-inflammatory; interferons fight viruses.

questions.stem: What causes her hypotension?
options: Massive vasodilation from too much TNF-α
Metaplasia of the smooth muscle in vessel walls
Hypertrophy of the heart limiting its filling
Too little histamine to keep the vessels open
questions.rationale: His answer to "what's the problem with too much TNF-α?": vasodilation, which is why it's called septic shock.

questions.stem: Which cytokines cause her lethargy and loss of appetite (sickness behavior)? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α together cause sickness behavior — lethargy, depression, malaise, poor appetite, sleepiness. IL-10 and TGF-β are anti-inflammatory.

questions.stem: Her fever is best explained by:
options: Low acute-phase proteins slowing her immune response
Complement lysing her red blood cells and releasing their contents into the blood
Cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF-α acting as endogenous pyrogens
Dystrophic calcification of the injured tissue
questions.rationale: IL-1 is an endogenous pyrogen ("if they give IL-1… there is a fever response"), and TNF-α also induces fever.

questions.stem: Which lab finding would you expect to rise as part of the acute-phase response?
questions.rationale: The liver makes acute-phase reactants — CRP, complement components, fibrinogen — during inflammation, and ESR rises.

clinical.title: Scenario 9 — Surgical unit
clinical.setting: Post-op day 7 after open abdominal surgery
clinical.text: A 59-year-old woman with a BMI of 41 had an open bowel resection. On post-op day 7, while coughing, she says she felt something "give," and the nurse sees the incision edges separating with serosanguineous drainage.

questions.stem: What has occurred?
questions.rationale: Wound separation = dehiscence, highest risk days 5–12, more likely with obesity and abdominal wounds. Evisceration is internal structures coming out after dehiscence.

questions.stem: The drainage is serosanguineous. This means:
options: Pus with many neutrophils and debris
Thick, fibrin-rich exudate from severe injury
questions.rationale: Serosanguineous = serous fluid with some blood. Purulent is pus; fibrinous is thick fibrin; sanguineous is very bloody.

questions.stem: Which are risk factors for her dehiscence named in the lecture? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Dehiscence risk peaks days 5–12, rises with obesity and abdominal wounds, and about half are associated with infection. Laparoscopic small incisions lower complications.

questions.stem: Which surgical approach did he say reduces complications like this?
options: Longer incisions that are easier to close
Leaving wounds open to heal by secondary intention
questions.rationale: "The smaller incisions you make, the less complications you have" — laparoscopic surgery.

questions.stem: On post-op day 7, a normally healing wound would be in which phase?
questions.rationale: Proliferative phase, days 3–14: fibroblasts laying down collagen, granulation tissue, angiogenesis, wound contraction.

clinical.title: Scenario 10 — Rapid rounds
clinical.text: Each item is a separate patient. Decide quickly, then check your reasoning against the slide in the key.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old's biopsy shows cervical cells varying in size and shape with disordered layers. The nurse anticipates the report will say:
questions.rationale: Variable size, shape and organization = dysplasia, common in the cervix; it can lead to neoplasm.

questions.stem: A patient's wound is 3 weeks old and still not closing, with dense lymphocytes and macrophages on biopsy. This is:
questions.rationale: More than 2 weeks, with lymphocyte and macrophage infiltration and incomplete healing, is chronic inflammation.

questions.stem: A patient with an allergic reaction has hives and flushing within minutes. Which mediator was released first?
questions.rationale: Mast-cell degranulation of histamine is very quick — dilation and permeability. Leukotrienes are made later and act longer.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term steroids asks how they reduce inflammation. Using the arachidonic acid pathway, corticosteroids act:
options: Early, at membrane phospholipids — before arachidonic acid is made
By activating complement to clear the inflamed tissue
By increasing histamine release from mast cells
Only on cyclooxygenase, like aspirin — after arachidonic acid is made
questions.rationale: Slide 67: corticosteroids block the step from membrane phospholipids to arachidonic acid; aspirin and NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase further down.

questions.stem: A burn patient's wound shows new capillaries and red, bumpy tissue on day 8. This tissue is:
questions.rationale: Granulation tissue — new capillaries, very red — fills the wound in the proliferative phase (days 3–14).

questions.stem: A 1-year-old surgical scar looks paler and flatter than it did at 3 months. Which phase explains this?
questions.rationale: Remodeling runs several weeks to 2 years — the scar reorganizes and "after a few months, it's completely gone" in appearance.

cards.back: Atrophy · hypertrophy · hyperplasia · metaplasia · dysplasia
Shrinkage in cell SIZE (not number); whole organ can shrink; less ER, fewer mitochondria
Disuse · denervation · loss of endocrine stimulation · inadequate nutrition · ischemia · aging
Increase in cell SIZE (not number); heart and kidney especially prone
Physiologic: skeletal muscle with exercise · Pathologic: cardiac hypertrophy from HTN

cards.front: Why is HTN cardiac hypertrophy bad?
cards.back: Wall gets so thick the ventricle can't fill — maladaptive
One kidney removed (pathologic) → other kidney enlarges (physiologic)
Increase in cell NUMBER (proliferation); can occur with hypertrophy
Hormonal — estrogen-dependent organs (breast, uterus)
Excess hormones/growth factors (endometrium) · viral — warts
Remove 70% of the liver → regenerates in ~2 weeks
Cells that don't divide — cardiac muscle, neurons
Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another (often less differentiated)
Smoker's trachea: ciliated columnar → squamous epithelium
Cells drop cilia to avoid the irritants, so nothing is caught anymore; gene switching → cancer risk
Deranged growth — cells vary in size, shape, organization; "atypical hyperplasia"; not truly adaptive
Cervix and respiratory tract; can lead to cancer

cards.front: Most common cause of cell injury
cards.back: Hypoxia
Ischemia (decreased blood flow)
ATP ↓ → Na⁺/K⁺ pump & Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange fail → cellular swelling, vacuolation
Uncharged atom/group with an unpaired electron (e.g., ROS); controlled by antioxidants
Lipid peroxidation · protein alteration · DNA alteration · mitochondria
More injury when flow returns: oxidative stress, ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺, inflammation, complement

qa.q: Name the biggest stressor you can put on yourself that actually improves your life?
qa.a: Exercise — a small stressor the cells adapt to. "What doesn't kill them makes them stronger."

qa.q: When you think about adaptation, do you think of it as good or bad?
qa.a: Generally good — but cells "aren't smart or dumb, they're just reacting," so some adaptations are pathologic (maladaptation).

qa.q: Can anybody give me an example of a physiologic adaptation?
qa.a: The class answer wasn't audible. He contrasted normal, needed changes with pathologic ones like muscle loss in starvation. (from slides 6–9: exercise hypertrophy, hormonal hyperplasia)

qa.q: Why is this [hypertrophied heart] a bad thing?
qa.a: The wall gets so thick the ventricle can't fill. Caused by hypertension — the heart adapts to beating against high pressure and makes things worse.

qa.q: Metaplasia — in what situation does this happen?
qa.a: Smoking — chronic irritation of the airway.

qa.q: Why are they getting rid of their cilia?
qa.a: The cilia grab everything that's inhaled; for a smoker that's toxic and injures the cells, so they drop the cilia to stop catching it.

qa.q: Is that adaptation or maladaptation for your body?
qa.a: Maladaptation — now nothing is being caught, even on a smoky day.

qa.q: What needs to happen inside the cell for ciliated cells to turn into non-ciliated cells?
qa.a: Genes are up- and down-regulated. Overdo it and you can get cancer — same idea with HPV/warts turning DNA segments on and off.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Name that atrophy — a hand that can't move after losing its nerve supply.
qa.a: Denervation.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Name that atrophy — a leg just out of a cast.
qa.a: Disuse.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Name that atrophy — menopause.
qa.a: Loss of endocrine stimulation.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Name that atrophy — a shrunken brain and kidney.
qa.a: Ischemia — both are heavily vascularized and prone to vascular events (e.g., stroke).

qa.q: (Kahoot) What adaptation does this image show?
qa.a: Dysplasia — he chose it because the cells "didn't look like the functional cells" (hyperplasia was also argued).

qa.q: Is inflammation a good thing or a bad thing?
qa.a: Generally good.

qa.q: When you sprain your ankle, why do they tell you to reduce the inflammation if it's good?
qa.a: Because it's nonspecific — the full response is more than a sprain needs, and limiting it can speed healing.

qa.q: Sprained ankle vs a venomous snake bite, 50,000 years ago — whose inflammation is most important?
qa.a: The snake bite — without inflammation that person might die. The sprain won't kill you; inflammation just makes the next weeks worse.

qa.q: Sprained ankle, no bleeding — what's the next step after hemostasis?
qa.a: Vasodilation — vessels get bigger; flow slows but more blood reaches the area, bringing what fights the injury.

qa.q: In a sprained ankle, is there any risk of bacteria?
qa.a: Not like a snake bite with venom — but immune cells still move in to clear dead cells and debris.

qa.q: (Kahoot) What is the correct timeline of inflammatory events?
qa.a: Vascular response (vasodilation, permeability) → leukocyte adhesion & migration → activation & phagocytosis. The cells have to leave the bloodstream to reach the damaged tissue.

qa.q: If plasma-derived mediators are always floating in our blood, are we always in an inflammatory state?
qa.a: No — they circulate inactive (proenzymes) and are activated only at the injury site.

qa.q: What process do [complement] help with in phagocytosis?
qa.a: Opsonization — marking the bacteria so phagocytes can eat them.

qa.q: A patient with a cirrhotic liver — what would you expect to see in these [plasma-derived] systems?
qa.a: A decrease — the liver makes them — so less complement and an increased infection rate.

qa.q: Anybody tell me the drug you take that decreases arachidonic acid [metabolites]?
qa.a: NSAIDs, aspirin. His hangover example: alcohol triggers a mini inflammatory response and headache; the pill in the morning helps.

qa.q: Mast cells release histamine — what does that cause?
qa.a: Allergy symptoms (more next week).

qa.q: What's one of the problems of having too much TNF-α?
qa.a: Vasodilation → septic shock.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which of these are plasma-derived mediators?
qa.a: Complement, clotting, kinin (from the liver).

qa.q: (Kahoot) What is the role of plasma-derived mediators?
qa.a: They're always circulating, waiting for an inflammatory response, and increase the inflammatory response once activated.

qa.q: (Kahoot) How does complement participate in inflammation?
qa.a: Opsonization, chemotaxis, lysis of bacteria (and anaphylatoxic activity).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which three cytokines are responsible for sickness behavior?
qa.a: IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α.

qa.q: What are the systemic manifestations of acute inflammation?
qa.a: With a big or long injury (a car accident, not a sprain): fever, sickness behavior/lethargy, more immune cells (leukocytosis), acute-phase proteins like CRP, and a raised ESR.

qa.q: (student asked) What about autoimmune disease?
qa.a: Autoimmunity causes cell injury, and that injury triggers inflammation — many treatments for autoimmunity and inflammation overlap (next week).

qa.q: Why do we make smaller incisions — what's it called?
qa.a: Laparoscopic surgery — the smaller the incisions, the fewer the complications (like dehiscence).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Fibroblasts divide during which phase of wound healing?
qa.a: The proliferative phase.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Put the phases of repair in order.
qa.a: Hemostasis, angiogenesis & granulation tissue → fibroblasts & extracellular matrix → maturation/remodeling.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Are sutures only for secondary intention?
qa.a: The answer wasn't clear in the recording. (from slide 85: primary intention = minimal tissue loss, edges close; sutures pull a wide wound together so it can heal that way.)
